Judaizing
JOO-day-ize-ing
verb / noun (the error of the Judaizers)
From “Judaize” (Greek ioudaizo, to live as a Jew); the error of the Judaizers, who would compel Gentile believers to keep the law of Moses for salvation.

Biblical Definition

Judaizing is the error of the Judaizers—those teachers in the apostolic age who would compel Gentile believers to be circumcised and to keep the law of Moses as necessary to salvation, in effect adding works of the law to the grace of Christ. It arose early: “certain men which came down from Judaea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.” Against this Paul waged his fiercest battle, for it struck at the heart of the gospel. He withstood Peter to the face at Antioch for compelling the Gentiles to live as Jews; he warned the Galatians, “if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing”; and he cried, “Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” The dictionary marks Judaizing as the archetype of every legalism that adds human works to the finished work of Christ. It is not the honouring of the law in its proper place, nor the embrace of the Jewish heritage of the faith; it is the fatal addition of the law's works to grace as a ground of acceptance with God—and the apostle pronounces such a gospel accursed. The dictionary holds the doctrine against its enduring forms: the Roman gospel of faith-plus-works anathematized at Trent, the legalism that makes rules and observances the measure of standing before God, and every scheme that, having begun in the Spirit, seeks to be perfected by the flesh. The remedy is the gospel Paul defended: a man is justified by faith in Christ alone, apart from the works of the law, and to add anything to Christ is to lose Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

The error of the Judaizers, who compelled Gentile believers to keep the law of Moses for salvation (Acts 15:1; Galatians 5:2); the archetype of every legalism that adds works to the finished work of Christ, against which Paul pronounced “accursed.”

JUDAIZING, verb / noun. [Greek ioudaizo, to live as a Jew.] Compelling Gentile believers to keep the law for salvation.

“Except ye be circumcised… ye cannot be saved” (Acts 15:1), the Judaizers' cry.

Paul withstood Peter for compelling Gentiles to live as Jews (Galatians 2:14).

“If ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing” (Galatians 5:2).

The archetype of every legalism that adds works to the finished work of Christ.

Key Scripture

Ga 2:14 — "But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?"

Ga 5:2 — "Behold, I Paul say unto you, that if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing."

Ac 15:1 — "And certain men which came down from Judaea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved."

Ga 3:3 — "Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?"

Modern Corruption

Judaizing is itself the corruption: the adding of works of the law to the grace of Christ as a ground of acceptance—the archetype of Rome's faith-plus-works and of every legalism that begins in the Spirit and seeks perfection by the flesh.

expand to see more

Judaizing is the corruption to be named, the archetypal assault on the gospel of grace. The Judaizers would compel Gentile believers to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses as necessary to salvation, adding the works of the law to the finished work of Christ. Paul saw that this struck at the heart of the gospel and fought it without quarter: he withstood Peter to the face, warned that the circumcised seeking justification by law had fallen from grace and that Christ should profit them nothing, and pronounced any other gospel accursed. To add the law's works to grace as a ground of acceptance is to lose Christ.

The dictionary marks Judaizing's enduring forms. Its purest modern heir is the Roman gospel of faith-plus-works anathematized at Trent; but the spirit appears wherever rules, observances, or human performance are made the measure of standing before God, and wherever believers who began in the Spirit seek to be perfected by the flesh. The dictionary distinguishes this fatal addition from the lawful honouring of God's law in its place and from the embrace of the faith's Jewish heritage; Judaizing is neither. It is legalism at the root, and the remedy is the gospel Paul defended: justification by faith in Christ alone, apart from the works of the law—for to add anything to Christ is to lose Him.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek ioudaizo (to live as a Jew, to adopt Jewish customs); the error of the Judaizers who bound the law of Moses upon Gentile believers for salvation.

expand to see more

Ioudaizo, Greek, “to live as a Jew,” to adopt Jewish observance (Galatians 2:14).

The Judaizers, teachers who bound circumcision and the law on Gentiles.

The error that adds the works of the law to the grace of Christ.

Refuted at the Jerusalem council and throughout Galatians.

The archetype of legalism and of Rome's faith-plus-works.

Usage

"The teacher named Judaizing the archetype of every legalism that adds works to Christ's finished work."

"He showed Paul pronouncing accursed any gospel that adds the law's works to grace."

"She distinguished honouring the law in its place from the Judaizing that makes it a ground of acceptance."
